processing: Single spring buds only, sorted strictly and delivered to the factory the same day. Once all handwork, it now combines machine steps with handwork at key stages, and aroma-lifting and final finishing are still done by hand.
harvest_season: Spring buds from February to April. The earliest, picked before the Hanshi festival just ahead of Qingming and called huo qian, are the most sought after.
appearance_dry: Tiny, sparrow-tongue buds, small and fine.
taste_profile: Rich and fresh, with a high lasting aroma and a mellow, clean finish.

brewing.notes: General advice for all-bud greens: cooler water and an uncovered glass or gaiwan. Hot water and a lid will flatten the aroma.

vintage_note: An early-market spring tea, sold as the current harvest and among the first Chinese greens of the year, ahead of Mengding teas, Long Jing and Bi Luo Chun. Buy the newest season and pay attention to picking date, since the earliest buds carry the premium.
description:
Pujiang Queshe is an all-bud green from Pujiang County on the southwestern edge of the Chengdu plain, named for buds as small as a sparrow's tongue. Its real selling point is earliness: it reaches the market ahead of the eastern China classics.

That timing comes from a mild climate and low hills at about 550 to 630 metres, which warm up early in the season. The picking rules are strict: single buds only, none picked in rain, none damaged, opened or hollow, and all at the factory on the same day.

The cup is a clear green with high fragrance and a mellow, fresh taste. All-bud tea scalds easily, so use cool water and watch it rather than the clock.

Queshe is a shape name used in many provinces, so look for Pujiang and for the geographical indication. Lüchangming Pujiang Queshe is a branded listing of the same tea, not a separate one.
history:
Local accounts say the tea was sent as tribute from the Song dynasty, grown around Baihe Temple and Datang. A legend credits the Southern Song scholar Wei Liaoweng with taking a liking to it at court, which is said to have made it a tribute tea.

Firmer ground comes in the Qing: a county gazetteer from the Qianlong era lists it among local products, and a Guangxu-era local record calls it fine and sweet-scented, and locally known as xi maojian. By the Republican period, 34 tea workshops made it, 17 of them at Chenjiaying, now Chengjia.

It grew into a leading Sichuan tea after the reform era. In this century production moved onto clean, mechanised lines at scale, and it has won first prizes at the Zhongcha Cup three times running.
